name: Iceland

facts.religion: Lutheran about 58% (church members), no religion growing

snapshot: Icelanders narrowly voted against reopening EU membership talks in August 2026, even as Trump's Greenland threats made them question their security.
culture: Iceland's sagas, written in the 13th century, are still readable by modern Icelanders, whose language has changed remarkably little. Icelanders use patronymic surnames and a public genealogy database. Björk, Sigur Rós and a remarkable crime-writing tradition are global exports. Christmas brings 13 mischievous Yule Lads.
society: Fishing and geothermal energy, which heats nearly all homes, underpin the economy, along with tourism and aluminium smelting. Iceland's banks collapsed in 2008, and it jailed bankers. It has no army and relies on NATO and a US defence pact. It regularly tops gender equality rankings.

story: Iceland, with 390,000 people, is the smallest country in NATO and the only one with no army. In 2008 its three big banks collapsed in one week, and in the wreckage it applied to join the EU, then dropped the bid in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came in. The reason it walked away then, and the reason it walked away again in 2026, is fish: fisheries are the backbone of the economy and Icelanders fear Brussels controlling their waters.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, a 38-year-old economist whose pro-EU coalition took power in late 2024, argued that the geopolitical moment had changed. Trump's threats to annex Greenland, Iceland's neighbour, made many Icelanders wonder whether NATO and a bilateral US defence pact were still enough (Journal-News/AP). She called a referendum, not on joining but on reopening talks, with a second vote promised on any final deal. On 29 August, Icelanders said no: 52.8 percent against, 47.2 percent for (NPR via WYPR). Worries about fishing quotas and giving up the króna for the euro outweighed the security case. Frostadóttir accepted the result and said the issue will not return before her term ends in 2028. Iceland remains in the European Economic Area and Schengen, already following, by her count, about 75 percent of EU rules without a vote on them. EU officials had hoped a yes would boost morale for the bloc's enlargement.
briefing.power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government with the confidence of the 63-seat Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments, founded in 930. The directly elected president is largely ceremonial.
briefing.holders: Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir (Social Democratic Alliance), since December 2024; President Halla Tómasdóttir.
